statements.statement: benchANT's YCSB results varied with read/write mix and used a Zipfian access pattern
statements.note: benchANT varied read share from 10% to 90% and used requestdistribution zipfian, with up to 50% differences.

statements.statement: The benchANT authors note that workload parameters and configuration affect the result
statements.note: Stated in the key insights section.

statements.statement: Percona independently reported different outcomes for read-only and mixed scenarios
statements.note: Percona's plgm tests: the read-only workload reached ~13.6k ops/sec and the 54/46 mixed workload ~8.7k, about 35% lower. This comes from a Percona page that the claim does not cite.

statements.statement: Capacity planning should use workload-specific evidence rather than a universal conversion factor
statements.note: This is an inference from the findings above; both sources show results vary by workload.

edits.rationale: The benchANT page varies the YCSB read/write mix with a Zipfian read pattern and says other workload parameters and configuration also matter. The Percona page, which the claim did not cite, reports a read-only baseline and a mixed workload with different capacity (~13.6k vs ~8.7k ops/sec). The planning advice is an inference from those findings.

edits.old: A read/write percentage is not a transferable MongoDB capacity multiplier: benchmark results depend on workload characteristics, query complexity, data and access patterns, and deployment configuration. (medium confidence)
edits.new: Benchmark results depend on workload characteristics, system architecture and configuration (Percona); benchANT likewise lists query complexity, number and size of records, access pattern, DBMS configuration and resources as parameters that affect performance alongside the read-write ratio. Percona's own test showed 46% writes cutting capacity by ~35% versus read-only, but that figure is specific to its environment. Sources: https://www.percona.com/blog/the-importance-of-realistic-benchmark-workloads/ ; https://benchant.com/blog/workload-read-write-ratio

evidence.quote: Ultimately, these tests reinforce an important reality: performance is not a fixed value. It is a moving target that depends entirely on workload characteristics, system architecture, and how the environment is configured and optimized.
Introducing 46% writes reduced capacity by ~35% compared to the read-only benchmark.
Read-write ratio appears on paper to be one of the most important workload parameters, along with query complexity and the number and size of records.
Each workload parameter can have a direct impact on database performance, as can the DBMS configuration and underlying resources.

evidence.quote: Following our baseline scenario, we conducted a mixed workload test (54% Reads, 46% Writes), using the same query definitions as the first workload.
The benchmarks were measured fully-automated with the benchANT benchmarking platform.
MongoDB shows only minor throughput changes with write-heavy and balanced read-write ratios.

statements.statement: Percona reports average read and write latency for its mixed workload
statements.note: The Workload #2 table has columns 'Avg Read Latency (ms)' and 'Avg Write Latency (ms)' (each under 40 characters, so quoted via the surrounding sentence).

statements.statement: benchANT tracks read and write 95th-percentile latency as well as aggregate throughput
statements.note: benchANT's KPI list is: the Throughput, the Read Latency (95% quantile), the Write Latency (95% quantile).

statements.statement: Capacity tests should retain separate read and write throughput and latency measures
statements.note: Recommendation inferred from the two practices above; benchANT reports that write latency and read latency respond differently to the write share.

edits.rationale: Percona's mixed-workload results table has separate Avg Read Latency and Avg Write Latency columns. benchANT lists throughput, read latency (95% quantile) and write latency (95% quantile) as its KPIs. The recommendation is an inference, and the benchANT part needed the benchANT page, which the claim did not cite.
